You pass if both lifetime answers name the shape of the code and the moment the window opens, and the exception answer says the process ends. Naming one lifetime case and the exception is a partial pass. Answering that rclcpp catches callback exceptions is a fail: it leads to code that relies on a node surviving a throw.

A ROS callback owns nothing by default: the only owner of an entity such as a subscription or a timer is the member holding its handle, and the only owner of whatever the callback touches is whatever its capture names, since the executor keeps no reference to it. Capturing
in a node is the one safe habit, because the entity and the state it uses are both members of one object and cannot outlive each other.

The problem these failures share is that they stay invisible in the ordinary case, reachable only once something that looks like configuration changes: a second thread, a second callback group, or shutdown catching a callback mid-flight. A node can pass every test run on one thread and still carry a callback that reads a destroyed object, throws past every safety net, or quietly runs at a fraction of its stated rate.

A class destroys its members in reverse declaration order, so an entity declared before the state its callback reads is destroyed after it, opening a window, during destruction, where the callback still runs against state already gone; one thread never reaches it, already returned from spinning first, but a second thread can be mid-callback while the first tears the node down. An exception leaving a callback is caught nowhere inside rclcpp: it unwinds out of the executor's loop, reaching

under one thread, and ending the process under more than one, since the language will not let an exception escape a thread's own function. An overrun timer is not queued and repaid; missed periods are dropped, so a slow callback settles at a lower rate with no error, unless the timer is asked how late it ran.

earns its reputation as the safe default and betrays it the moment a lambda reaches past the node itself, to a local, a raw pointer handed in from outside, or a member of another object nobody promised would still exist. A second executor thread or one more callback group touches no line of the node's logic, yet reaches a destruction order or a throw a single-threaded test cannot.

You meet this in the interview question itself: naming two shapes of a callback reading an object that is gone, and saying, without hedging, that an exception out of any callback ends the process rather than being logged, whether from a subscription or a timer.
